books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Figures from the Provost Marshal General’s report, as summarized in the 1956 report Veterans in Our Society (U.S. Government Printing Office). Figures are rounded.
stimulus.text:
Results of the four drafts under the Enrollment Act of 1863.

| Outcome | Men |
| Names drawn | 776,829 |
| Men who furnished substitutes | 73,607 |
| Men who paid $300 commutation | 86,724 |
| Men exempted | 315,509 |
| Men who failed to report | 161,244 |
| Men who entered the army as draftees | 46,347 |

Altogether 119,954 men entered the army under the act: 46,347 draftees plus 73,607 hired substitutes. The rows overlap, so they do not add to the total drawn.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: A drafted man could pay $300 to escape service or hire a substitute. That rule fed the New York City draft riots of July 1863 mainly because it

options.text: required every man in New York City to serve in the army.
options.misconception: Background: the draft called men by district quotas, and most men drawn escaped service; it did not require every man to serve.

options.text: let wealthy men buy their way out while working-class men faced the draft.
freed enslaved people living in New York City at once.
options.misconception: Background: the Enrollment Act said nothing about freeing enslaved people; New York had already ended slavery in 1827.

options.text: banned all substitutes from serving in the army.
options.misconception: Background: the act expressly allowed a drafted man to furnish an acceptable substitute.

rationales.A: Background: the draft called men by district quotas, and most men drawn escaped service; it did not require every man to serve.
rationales.C: Background: the Enrollment Act said nothing about freeing enslaved people; New York had already ended slavery in 1827.
rationales.D: Background: the act expressly allowed a drafted man to furnish an acceptable substitute.
rationales.B: The 300 dollar commutation fee was beyond most working-class men, so the draft looked like a rich man’s escape and a poor man’s burden.
rationales.general:
1. The table shows the escape hatches: 86,724 paid commutation and 73,607 furnished substitutes.
2. Both hatches cost money, and 300 dollars was a working man’s fortune.
3. Background: in New York City in July 1863, protesters first attacked draft offices, then turned on Black residents.
4. A draft that the rich can buy out of feels like a tax on the poor.
Remember: when a law sells exemptions, ask who can afford to buy one.
